scenes.script_line: By now, you've learned the six human needs: Certainty. Variety. Significance. Love and connection. Growth. And contribution. These needs influence all of us. And they don't disappear when you come to work. They influence how you respond to change. How you communicate. What motivates you. And what frustrates you. The more you understand what drives you, the more choice you have in how you respond.
scenes.visual_direction: Varied dignified people working in varied environments: land work outdoors, technical hands-on work, a small planning meeting, a team together, one person focused alone.

scenes.script_line: Let's start with certainty. At work, certainty can mean wanting clear expectations, reliable systems, and knowing what success looks like. But when certainty becomes too important, change can feel threatening. A new process. A different schedule. A new way of doing something. Instead of asking "Why are we changing this?" ask "What do I need to understand so I can adapt?" You can create certainty through preparation, communication, organization, and skill.
scenes.visual_direction: Order first: checklist ticked, schedule on wall, tidy organized workspace. Then a change arrives and a worker adapts calmly, re-planning without panic.

scenes.script_line: Then there is variety. Some people love new problems, new projects, and different tasks. That can bring creativity and energy to a team. But too much variety can become distraction. Starting lots of things. Getting bored with routine. Or changing a process before it has had time to work. Ask yourself: "How can I create healthy challenge without creating unnecessary chaos?" Learn something new. Improve a process. But remember: not everything needs to change just because change feels exciting.
scenes.visual_direction: Energy of variety: switching between tasks, a lively idea exchange; then returning to one task and finishing it properly, tools down, job complete.

scenes.script_line: Significance is the need to feel that we matter. At work, this can mean wanting recognition, responsibility, or knowing that your work has value. You can seek significance by needing credit, proving yourself, or needing to be right. Or you can meet it through excellence. Reliability. Solving problems. And making a contribution that genuinely matters. Instead of asking "Do people notice me?" ask "Am I creating value?"
scenes.visual_direction: Contrast: someone performing for attention versus a quiet excellent worker solving a real problem with skill. Dignity in mastery, not noise.

scenes.script_line: Connection is also a powerful need. Most of us want to feel that we belong and that people respect us. Healthy connection is built through trust. Listening. Helping each other. Showing appreciation. And communicating honestly. But the need for connection can make us avoid difficult conversations. We may stay quiet because we don't want someone to be upset with us. Real connection does not mean agreeing all the time. Strong teams can disagree and still respect one another.
scenes.visual_direction: Real connection at work: two people collaborating, one helping another, attentive listening, a respectful disagreement that ends resolved with a handshake or nod.

scenes.script_line: Growth is the need to learn and become more capable. At work, this might mean learning a new skill. Asking for feedback. Improving how you communicate. Or becoming better at something you already do. When work feels repetitive, ask: "What can I learn from this?" "What can I become better at?" Growth does not always have to come from someone else. It is something you can take ownership of.
scenes.visual_direction: Learning in motion: apprentice watching a mentor, practicing a technique, reading a manual or instructions, receiving feedback and applying it, visible improvement.

scenes.script_line: And finally, contribution. Contribution is the need to give beyond ourselves. At work, it can be as simple as helping someone. Sharing what you know. Improving a process for the next person. Or solving a problem before it becomes someone else's problem. Contribution changes the question from "What am I getting from this?" to "What am I adding?" And that shift can change the experience of work.
scenes.visual_direction: Quiet generosity: helping unasked, teaching a colleague, tidying or improving a shared space, setting up tools and materials ready for the next shift.

scenes.script_line: None of these needs are good or bad. What matters is how we choose to meet them. Certainty can make you prepared, or resistant to change. Variety can make you creative, or distracted. Significance can lead to excellence, or ego. Connection can build trust, or make you afraid to speak honestly. Growth can make you curious and capable. Contribution can turn work into something bigger than yourself.
scenes.visual_direction: Montage across one working day: order and checklists, task variety, quiet mastery, human connection, learning, and generous contribution — varied dignified roles.

scenes.onscreen: No need is good or bad. How you meet it is.

shots.text: morning: checklist and tidy yard
midday: varied tasks, a crew at work
quiet mastery: close on hands at a fine task
evening: colleagues sharing water, laughing

scenes.script_line: Think about your own work. Which two needs influence you most? How do they help you? And how might they sometimes get in your way? Then ask: "What is a healthier way I can meet this need while also helping the team?" Self-awareness gives you choice. You cannot always control what happens around you. But you can understand what drives you. Choose how you respond. And use your needs in a way that helps you grow, and helps the people around you grow too.
scenes.visual_direction: Reflection: a person alone pausing to think and write in a notebook, then standing and rejoining colleagues warmly, direction found.
